sections.heading: Remembering where you have placed me
sections.text: Heavenly Father, you have put me inside the church that your Son bought with his own blood. I do not belong to myself, and I do not stand alone. Please keep giving me grace upon grace so that the life I live matches the calling you have given me in Christ.
theological_themes: The believer’s calling is received within the redeemed people of God, not as a private spiritual project.
Christ’s blood secures the church, and God’s grace enables a life worthy of that calling.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the church as belonging to God because it was obtained through Christ’s blood. This grounds the prayer’s sense of belonging to a redeemed people rather than merely choosing a religious community.

Paul urges believers to walk in a manner worthy of their calling, especially in humility and unity within the body. This directly supports the request to live faithfully in the vocation God has given.

sections.heading: Trusting you to carry me home
sections.text: I am traveling through a world that often feels like rough water. Keep me safe in Christ, like someone sheltered in an ark, and bring me through every storm until I reach the safe harbor of your eternal rest.
theological_themes: Life in this world is a pilgrimage marked by trouble, but God preserves his people in Christ.
The believer’s hope is not escape from all storms now, but safe arrival in God’s eternal rest.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus tells his disciples to expect trouble in the world while taking heart because he has overcome it. This supports the prayer’s confidence that present turmoil is real but not ultimate.
Hebrews speaks of a remaining Sabbath rest for the people of God and calls believers to persevere toward it. That gives biblical shape to the image of being brought into the harbor of eternal rest.

sections.heading: Asking you to make me fruitful
sections.text: You have planted me in your vineyard. Do not let me become all leaves and no fruit, impressive on the outside but empty before you. Cut away what is useless in me. Remove what only drains life and feeds pride. Water what you have planted with your blessing, and make me fruitful in ways that please you.
theological_themes: God is the planter and keeper of his people; fruitfulness depends on his life-giving work.
Spiritual pruning may be painful, but it is an act of grace meant to produce real holiness rather than outward appearance.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus presents the Father as the vinedresser who prunes fruitful branches so that they bear more fruit, while life and fruitfulness come from abiding in Christ. This is the central biblical background for the prayer’s vineyard language.

Isaiah’s vineyard song warns against the tragedy of receiving God’s care yet producing corrupt fruit. It illuminates the prayer’s fear of having leaves or wild grapes instead of the fruit God desires.

sections.heading: Being faithful to Christ, not flirting with the world
sections.text: I am part of the bride of the Lamb, your church. Make me faithful to Christ: loyal, pure, loving, devoted, and true. Do not let my deepest loves play games with the world or give themselves to what cannot last. Lift my heart above temporary things. Let your love be enough for me, your glory be my joy, your commands be the road I walk, and the cross of Christ be the place where I rest.
theological_themes: The church belongs to Christ as his bride and is called to covenant faithfulness and purity.
Love for the world competes with love for God, so the believer asks for ordered affections and rest in the cross.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes Christ loving the church, giving himself for her, and cleansing her so she may be holy. This supports the prayer’s identity as part of Christ’s bride and the desire for purity.
Paul speaks of presenting the church as a pure bride to Christ and warns against being led away from sincere devotion to him. This closely matches the prayer’s concern about divided affections.
John warns that love for the world and love for the Father are incompatible, and that the world is passing away. This grounds the request to live above the love of temporary things.

sections.heading: Resting in redemption while I wait for heaven
sections.text: Father, my heart is not always burning with love for you. I get tired, cold, distracted, and dull. But I rest in the redemption your Son has already won. And I look ahead to the day when I will be with you fully—when weariness will not weigh me down, sin will not cool my love, unbelief will not cloud my sight, and zeal for you will never run out.
theological_themes: The believer honestly confesses spiritual weakness while resting in Christ’s finished redemption.
Heaven is the hope of perfected love, clear sight, freedom from sin, and unwearied worship.

scripture_references.connection: Paul gives language for the believer’s grief over remaining sin while pointing to deliverance through Jesus Christ. This helps frame the prayer’s honesty about coldness and weakness without despair.

Revelation promises God’s dwelling with his people and the end of death, mourning, crying, and pain. This supports the prayer’s forward look to a life with God where present burdens no longer oppress.
Paul contrasts present partial sight with the future fullness of knowing God. This illuminates the prayer’s hope that the dimming mist of unbelief will finally be gone.

sections.heading: Letting these hopes steady me
sections.text: Father, let these truths hold me up today. When I am weak, let them be a support under my soul. When I am afraid or tired, let them comfort me. Keep me living from what Christ has done, what you are making me, and where you are bringing me.
theological_themes: Christian perseverance is sustained by gospel truth, future hope, and the Father’s faithful keeping.
Comfort comes not from self-confidence but from God’s saving work and promises.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews describes God’s promise as strong encouragement and an anchor for the soul, secured in the heavenly hope opened by Jesus. This fits the prayer’s request that these truths steady and comfort the believer.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses the language of the church as the Lamb’s bride. This is biblically grounded, but in an individual prayer it requires care so the speaker does not imagine themselves as the whole bride, but as a member of the church that is Christ’s bride.

The phrase about not letting strong affection “dally with the world” reflects Puritan concern about worldliness. I preserved the force as divided loves and flirtation with what cannot last, without turning it into rejection of ordinary created goods as evil in themselves.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “vocation” primarily as the Christian calling to belong to Christ and live worthily within his church, not as a modern career or job calling.

I kept the original concrete images—voyager, ark, harbor, vineyard, pruning, wild grapes, bride, cross as resting place—but recast them in conversational language so they could be prayed naturally today.

I rendered “no langour shall oppress” as freedom from weariness and spiritual dullness, since the original seems to refer not merely to physical tiredness but to the heaviness that weakens love, zeal, and worship.
